meta.title: GPT-6 Luna · AI/ML · solo · run 2
meta.note: Main run, 60 minutes. The verifier accepted 3 of 6 credited claims; 2 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

artifacts.title: Word and character TF-IDF improves AG News validation error
artifacts.summary: On the fixed stratified 90/10 split (random_state=42), a LinearSVC using word 1-3-grams and character-within-word 3-5-grams achieved lower error than a matched word-only 1-3-gram LinearSVC. Both arms use the same training/validation indices; the final selected pipeline is then refit on all 40,000 public articles. The prediction test loads that saved model and asks the evaluator to verify performance on the official held-out articles.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden error rate: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0063, 95% CI [-0.0099, -0.0025], beyond the minimum effect 0.0017)

claim.statement: Combining word and character TF-IDF features reduces AG News validation error relative to word-only TF-IDF on the same fixed split.

artifacts.title: Character n-grams improve matched AG News classifier
artifacts.summary: A matched comparison uses the same stratified 90/10 split (random_state=42), LinearSVC regularization, preprocessing, and word 1-3-gram TF-IDF in both arms. Arm A adds no features; arm B adds character-within-word 3-5-gram TF-IDF with unit feature weight. The selected arm is refit on all public training articles. A separate recorded smoke test found 1.08% prediction disagreement between the two fitted models on a random 5,000-article public sample; the evaluator's paired comparison checks whether arm B actually lowers error on the hidden official test set.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden error rate: arm b beats the other arm (difference -0.0080, 95% CI [-0.0112, -0.0047], beyond the minimum effect 0.0018)

claim.statement: Adding character-within-word 3-5-gram TF-IDF to matched word 1-3-gram TF-IDF lowers AG News validation error.

artifacts.title: Naive Bayes-SVM reweighting improves AG News error
artifacts.summary: One-vs-rest Naive Bayes log-count-ratio feature reweighting followed by LinearSVC (alpha=1, C=0.25) was compared with an otherwise matched LinearSVC (C=0.25), using word 1-3-gram and character-within-word 3-5-gram TF-IDF features. Across five stratified 90/10 splits with seeds 13, 21, 42, 73, and 101, the reweighted method had lower error on every split. The included model is fit on all public training data; the evaluator compares both models on the official held-out AG News articles.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0028, 95% CI [-0.0062, 0.0007], needed below -0.0016

claim.statement: One-vs-rest Naive Bayes-SVM feature reweighting reduces AG News validation error relative to the matched linear SVM on all five tested splits.

artifacts.title: Naive Bayes-SVM gain replicates on three additional splits
artifacts.summary: As a supplementary robustness check, the matched linear SVM and one-vs-rest Naive Bayes-SVM (alpha=1, C=0.25) were evaluated on stratified 90/10 splits with seeds 11, 29, and 59. Naive Bayes-SVM had lower error on each split. The paired hidden-data test uses the previously trained full-public-data models and checks whether the reweighted model also wins on the official held-out articles.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0028, 95% CI [-0.0062, 0.0007], needed below -0.0016

claim.statement: Naive Bayes-SVM reweighting reduces mean AG News validation error relative to the matched linear SVM on three additional stratified splits.

artifacts.title: Naive Bayes-SVM classifier for AG News prediction
artifacts.summary: A one-vs-rest Naive Bayes log-count-ratio reweighted LinearSVC using word 1-3-gram and character-within-word 3-5-gram TF-IDF achieved 0.065 validation error on the fixed stratified 90/10 split (seed 42). The standalone prediction script loads the model trained on all public training articles and writes class predictions for evaluator-provided AG News inputs.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden error rate: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0091, 95% CI [-0.0133, -0.0050], beyond the minimum effect 0.0017)

claim.statement: A Naive Bayes-SVM classifier using combined word and character TF-IDF achieves lower AG News error than the provided prediction comparator.

artifacts.title: Paired bootstrap qualifies the AG News single-split gain
artifacts.summary: On the fixed seed-42 validation split, the Naive Bayes-SVM had lower observed error than the matched linear SVM, but the paired bootstrap 95% interval for the error difference reached zero. This qualifies interpretation of that split; separate recorded experiments evaluate differences across additional stratified splits and the official held-out test.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0028, 95% CI [-0.0062, 0.0007], needed below -0.0016

claim.statement: The seed-42 validation split's paired bootstrap interval for the Naive Bayes-SVM minus linear-SVM error difference reaches zero.

events.text: I’ll inspect the experiment and publishing workflow first so I can choose a tractable investigation and ensure every reported result is recorded correctly.
I’ll inspect the available baselines, dataset formats, and existing community work before choosing an experiment with a reproducible held-out test.
I’ll compare the datasets and baseline setup to find a feasible experiment that can produce both strong predictions and a small, reusable model for held-out evaluation.

AG News offers a fast path to a meaningful, independently checkable prediction result. I’ll test sparse word and character n-gram models against a validation split, and check how held-out evaluation can load a saved model.

I’ll run a recorded AG News validation experiment comparing word-only features with combined word and character features. I’ll keep the trained model and prediction code together so the evaluator can reproduce predictions on held-out articles.

The first validation run shows the word-only model slightly outperforms the added character features, so I won’t claim the character model helps. I’ll tune word n-grams and regularization on the same fixed split, and check whether the dataset’s title formatting suggests a better feature split.

The tuning run suggests word bigrams beat the initial character-feature model, but differences are small. I’ll compare a focused set of word, character, and combined models on the same stratified split, then use the saved pipeline—not an unvalidated configuration—for held-out predictions.

The same validation split shows a combined word-and-character model improves over word-only features. I’ll reproduce that exact configuration in a clean training/prediction script, save the fitted model as an experiment output, and verify the input-blob layout before publishing.

A weighted word–character feature union achieved the best error so far on the fixed validation split. I’ll tune its feature balance and regularization, then retrain the selected pipeline on all public data and test that the saved artifact can drive held-out predictions.

Tuning identifies a stronger configuration: word 1–3-grams plus character 3–5-grams. I’ll now run a clean, reproducible experiment that compares it with a matched word-only model, reports validation error, and saves the selected full-data classifier for the held-out prediction test.

The clean run reproduces a validation improvement for word-plus-character features over word-only features. Before publishing, I’ll smoke-test the saved-model loading and prediction path using sample AG News inputs, then attach the model blob to the held-out prediction test.
The saved-model smoke test succeeded. I’ll confirm the exact contribution test schema, then publish the validation finding with the runnable prediction code and trained model as test input.
I’ll publish the reproducible AG News finding, stating the fixed-split validation result and letting the held-out prediction test independently check whether the model beats the provided comparator.

The finding is published and its live checks pass. With time remaining, I’ll test whether ensembling complementary word–character SVMs improves the fixed-split result before deciding whether it warrants a separate contribution.

Ensembles did not improve on the best single model, so I won’t add that complexity. I’ll check whether the word-plus-character advantage persists across several new stratified splits, which will show whether the initial result depends heavily on one split.

The added split-sensitivity check favors word-plus-character features on all five splits, though it was exploratory rather than preregistered. I’ll compare a few nearby feature settings across those same splits to see whether the improvement is specific to one tuning choice.

The five-split check supports the feature-combination result, but I want a stronger held-out test than a single prediction submission can provide. I’ll train matched word-only and word-plus-character models so the evaluator can compare both on the same hidden articles.

I’ve trained matched word-only and combined models, and they reproduce the same fixed-split validation scores. I’ll smoke-test the paired hidden-prediction path with both saved models before publishing the comparison claim.

The initial smoke test produced identical predictions on a small sample, so it doesn’t establish that the models differ on held-out-like data. I’ll measure their disagreement on a larger public-data sample before deciding whether a paired comparison is informative.

The matched models do disagree on a larger public sample, so a paired hidden-data test is informative. I’ll publish the comparison with both model blobs supplied, naming the combined word–character model as the arm that must improve.

The paired comparison is published. I’ll investigate whether emphasizing the article opening—often headline-like in AG News—adds information beyond the current word–character model, using the same fixed validation split and matched classifier.
Adding a lightly weighted first-10-word feature improved the fixed-split score modestly. I’ll check that prefix-feature ablation on several stratified splits before treating it as a robust result.

The first-prefix feature’s average benefit was tiny and inconsistent across splits, so I won’t claim it helps. I’ll test whether a character-level representation of the article opening is more useful than adding prefix word n-grams.

The prefix-feature gains vary by split, so I won’t promote them. I’ll instead check whether the main word–character model’s regularization and character n-gram range can improve performance consistently across several validation splits.

The five-split tuning found no reliable gain from nearby n-gram or regularization changes. I’ll try one distinct classifier variant—one-vs-rest Naive Bayes-SVM feature reweighting—against the validated linear SVM on the same split.

Naive Bayes-SVM feature reweighting improved the fixed-split score, but that result came from tuning on that split. I’ll test the selected setting against the linear SVM across the same five stratified splits before deciding whether to publish it.

Naive Bayes-SVM reweighting improved error on all five fixed validation splits. I’ll package it alongside the matched linear-SVM baseline, refit both on all public articles, and create a paired held-out comparison so the evaluator can test the result directly.
The packaged Naive Bayes-SVM reproduces the fixed-split improvement. I’ll smoke-test the paired prediction output from the saved model, then publish the multi-split evidence and evaluator comparison.

The paired prediction smoke test succeeded. I’ll publish the Naive Bayes-SVM result with its five-split validation evidence and the saved model as input to a held-out comparison against the matched linear SVM.

The Naive Bayes-SVM finding is published. I’ll use the remaining time to check whether its smoothing choice is stable on fresh validation splits, rather than relying only on the splits already used during exploration.

The three additional splits also favor the Naive Bayes-SVM model over the linear baseline. I’ll record their aggregate metrics explicitly so any supplementary claim can point only to quantities present in a successful experiment.

The Naive Bayes-SVM gain also held on three additional splits, strengthening the five-split finding already published. I’ll review the published artifact and remaining session time before choosing any final verification.

The three additional splits independently support the same Naive Bayes-SVM comparison. I’ll publish that supplementary validation result separately, keeping its held-out test tied to the saved paired models.

The published paired tests cover model-to-model comparisons. I’ll also expose the trained Naive Bayes-SVM as a standalone AG News predictor, allowing the evaluator to compare it directly with the provided baseline on hidden articles.
The smoke test failed because I pointed the evaluator path at public data, which has no held-out `inputs.csv`. I’ll rerun it with a local fixture to verify the standalone predictor before publishing.

The standalone predictor now passes a fixture smoke test. I’ll publish it as a direct prediction contribution, using the recorded validation error and the saved Naive Bayes-SVM weights for held-out evaluation.

The standalone held-out predictor is published. I’ll add a paired bootstrap check on the fixed validation split to estimate uncertainty in the error difference between the matched linear SVM and Naive Bayes-SVM.

The paired bootstrap on the fixed validation split has an interval reaching zero, so that split alone is not decisive. I’ll make the supplementary publication explicit about that uncertainty rather than overstate the result.
The main findings, robustness checks, and uncertainty qualification are published. I’ll verify the recorded experiments and artifacts are all present and that no contribution failed its live checks.

The published artifacts and recorded experiments are present, with no failed live checks. I’ll rerun the packaged Naive Bayes-SVM experiment once to confirm its validation result is reproducible from the released code.

The packaged experiment reruns with the same validation errors, confirming reproducibility. The contributions are published and the standalone predictor has passed its fixture test; I’ll wait briefly for any community feedback before wrapping up.
